{{distinguish|Synchronizing word}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:''k''-synchronized sequence}}
In [[mathematics]] and [[theoretical computer science]], a '''''k''-synchronized sequence''' is an infinite [[sequence]] of terms ''s''(''n'') characterized by a [[Finite-state machine|finite automaton]] taking as input two strings ''m'' and ''n'', each expressed in some fixed [[Radix|base]] ''k'', and accepting if ''m''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''s''(''n''). The class of ''k''-synchronized sequences lies between the classes of [[Automatic sequence|''k''-automatic sequences]] and [[k-regular sequence|''k''-regular sequences]].

==Definitions==

===As relations===
Let Σ be an alphabet of ''k'' symbols where ''k''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;2, and let [''n'']<sub>''k''</sub> denote the base-''k'' representation of some number ''n''. Given ''r''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;2, a subset ''R'' of <math>\mathbb{N}^{r}</math> is ''k''-synchronized if the relation {([''n''<sub>1</sub>]<sub>''k''</sub>, ..., [''n''<sub>''r''</sub>]<sub>''k''</sub>)} is a right-synchronized<ref>{{citation | last1 = Frougny | first1 = C. | last2 = Sakarovitch | first2 = J. | title = Synchronized rational relations of finite and infinite words | journal = Theoret. Comput. Sci. | volume = 108 | year = 1993 | pages = 45–82 | doi=10.1016/0304-3975(93)90230-Q | doi-access =  }}</ref> [[Rational set#Rational relations and rational functions|rational relation]] over Σ<sup>&lowast;</sup>&nbsp;×&nbsp;...&nbsp;×&nbsp;Σ<sup>&lowast;</sup>, where (''n''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''n''<sub>''r''</sub>) <math>\in</math> ''R''.<ref name=CM>Carpi & Maggi (2010)</ref>

===Language-theoretic===
Let ''n''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;0 be a [[natural number]] and let ''f'': <math>\mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}</math> be a map, where both ''n'' and ''f''(''n'') are expressed in base ''k''. The sequence ''f''(''n'') is ''k''-synchronized if the language of pairs <math>\{(n, f(n))\}</math> is [[Regular language|regular]].

==History==
The class of ''k''-synchronized sequences was introduced by Carpi and Maggi.<ref name=CM />

==Example==

===Subword complexity===
Given a ''k''-automatic sequence ''s''(''n'') and an infinite string ''S''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''s''(1)''s''(2)..., let ρ<sub>''S''</sub>(n) denote the subword complexity of ''S''; that is, the number of distinct [[Substring|subwords]] of length ''n'' in ''S''. Goč, Schaeffer, and Shallit<ref>{{cite book | last1 = Goč | first1 = D. | last2 = Schaeffer | first2 = L. | last3 = Shallit | first3 = J. | others = Editors Béal MP., Carton O. | title = Subword complexity and ''k''-synchronization | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science | volume=7907 | location=Berlin | publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] | year=2013 | isbn=978-3-642-38770-8 }}</ref> demonstrated that there exists a finite automaton accepting the language
:<math>
\{(n, m)_k \mid n \geq 0 \text{ and } m = \rho_S(n)\}.
</math>
This automaton guesses the endpoints of every contiguous block of symbols in ''S'' and verifies that each subword of length ''n'' starting within a given block is novel while all other subwords are not. It then verifies that ''m'' is the sum of the sizes of the blocks. Since the pair (''n'',&nbsp;''m'')<sub>''k''</sub> is accepted by this automaton, the subword [[complexity function]] of the ''k''-automatic sequence ''s''(''n'') is ''k''-synchronized.

==Properties==
''k''-synchronized sequences exhibit a number of interesting properties. A non-exhaustive list of these properties is presented below.
*Every ''k''-synchronized sequence is [[k-regular sequence|''k''-regular]].<ref name=CM26>Carpi & Maggi (2010), Proposition 2.6</ref>
*Every [[Automatic sequence|''k''-automatic sequence]] is ''k''-synchronized. To be precise, a sequence ''s''(''n'') is ''k''-automatic if and only if ''s''(''n'') is ''k''-synchronized and ''s''(''n'') takes on finitely many terms.<ref name=CM28>Carpi & Maggi (2010), Proposition 2.8</ref> This is an immediate consequence of both the above property and the fact that every ''k''-regular sequence taking on finitely many terms is ''k''-automatic.
*The class of ''k''-synchronized sequences is closed under termwise sum and termwise composition.<ref name=CM21>Carpi & Maggi (2010), Proposition 2.1</ref><ref name=CM22>Carpi & Maggi (2010), Proposition 2.2</ref>
*The terms of any ''k''-synchronized sequence have a linear growth rate.<ref name=CM25>Carpi & Maggi (2010), Proposition 2.5</ref>
*If ''s''(''n'') is a ''k''-synchronized sequence, then both the subword complexity of ''s''(''n'') and the palindromic complexity of ''s''(''n'') (similar to subword complexity, but for distinct [[palindrome]]s) are ''k''-regular sequences.<ref>{{citation | last1 = Carpi | first1 = A. | last2 = D'Alonzo | first2 = V. | title = On factors of synchronized sequences | journal = Theoret. Comput. Sci. | volume = 411 | issue = 44–46 | year = 2010 | pages = 3932–3937 | doi=10.1016/j.tcs.2010.08.005 | doi-access =  }}</ref>
